pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

## zotero-research

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents

Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups

- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

### memory milvus lock misdiagnosis
When memsearch fails to open `~/.memsearch/milvus.db`, milvus-lite prints:

> Failed to open the local Milvus Lite database. If this database was created with an older Milvus Lite release, it may not be compatible with Milvus Lite 3.x. Move the existing .db file aside, then rebuild the index...

**That text is a generic open-failure string, not a version verdict.** It fires just as readily on plain lock contention. Diagnosed 2026-08-14: the underlying error was `BlockingIOError: [Errno 35]` from `flock`, and `lsof +D ~/.memsearch/milvus.db` named the holder — a concurrent manual `memsearch index` running after the SecondBrain vault move. The same DB with the same milvus-lite 3.1.1 had indexed successfully hours earlier.

(Attribution caution: at the time this was written the holder was assumed to be "another Claude session," inferred from an unfamiliar PID and shell-snapshot id. Eric corrected that — it was not. `lsof` tells you *which process*, never *which agent or person*; state the process and leave the actor unnamed.)

**Why:** following the message's advice (move the .db aside, rebuild) throws away a working index and costs an hours-scale re-index of the SecondBrain library — a self-inflicted outage in response to a transient collision.

**How to apply:**
- Before believing any milvus-lite "incompatible database" message, run `lsof +D ~/.memsearch/milvus.db` and `ps aux | grep memsearch`. A live holder means wait, not rebuild.
- Milvus Lite is single-writer. `daily-backup.ps1`'s advisory lock (`.memsearch-index.lock`, ~line 416) coordinates the nightly reindex with the SessionEnd hook only — it cannot see a hand-run `memsearch index`, so manual indexing during a backup window collides. Avoid running `memsearch index` by hand while the nightly backup may fire.
- `memsearch-index:full-set` in `.errors.log` is therefore usually transient. Confirm the lock is free, then let the next scheduled run clear it.

**Tooling mitigation added 2026-08-14 (because the written warning was not enough).** Later the same day a session ran `memsearch reset --yes` anyway and triggered a ~2h full rebuild — the exact outage this note warns about, with the note already on disk. Prose guidance does not survive contact with a scary error message, so the guard is now in code:

- `~/.local/bin/ms-search` — lock-aware retry wrapper for reads (`search` / `stats` / `expand` / `transcript`; write subcommands are refused). Retries with backoff to 60s (`MS_SEARCH_MAX_WAIT`), then exits **75** saying the DB is healthy and not to run `reset`. It retries **only** on `DataDirLockedError` / `another process holds the lock` / `Resource temporarily unavailable` / `_acquire_lock` / `fcntl.flock`; it deliberately does **not** key on the "may not be compatible with Milvus Lite 3.x" sentence, since that same wording is emitted for genuine incompatibility — so real corruption still fails fast and passes its exit code through.

The compiler at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/` has three stages. Each fails

When memsearch fails to open `~/.memsearch/milvus.db`, milvus-lite prints:

> Failed to open the local Milvus Lite database. If this database was created with an older Milvus Lite release, it may not be compatible with Milvus Lite 3.x. Move the existing .db file aside, then rebuild the index...

When memsearch fails to open `~/.memsearch/milvus.db`, milvus-lite prints:

> Failed to open the local Milvus Lite database. If this database was created with an older Milvus Lite release, it may not be compatible with Milvus Lite 3.x. Move the existing .db file aside, then rebuild the index...

**That text is a generic open-failure string, not a version verdict.** It fires just as readily on plain lock contention. ### memory compiler pipeline
The compiler at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/` has three stages. Each fails
differently and the symptoms look alike, so identify the stage before fixing.

**Stage 1 — `hooks/session-end.py`.** Writes `scripts/session-flush-<uuid>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>.md`,
then spawns `flush.py`. Logs every firing to `scripts/flush.log` as `SessionEnd fired`.
If `flush.log` has no such line for days but the hook works when run by hand, sessions
are being *closed* rather than exited cleanly — not a config break. Self-verifying: end
one session normally and re-check the tail.

**Stage 2 — `scripts/flush.py`.** Calls the Agent SDK, appends to `daily/<date>.md`, writes
`scripts/last-flush.json` **only on success**, and **deletes its context file on success**.
Therefore **every leftover `session-flush-*.md` is a flush that died**, and its datestamp
maps to a missing `daily/<date>.md`. That is the cheapest diagnostic in the whole system —
count the leftovers. A stale `last-flush.json` means flushes are *dying*, not that the hook
never fired. Recover one by hand:
`uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/flush.py <context-file> <session-id> [YYYY-MM-DD]`
Success = `Result: FLUSH_OK` + `Flush complete` in `flush.log`.

**The third arg is a backfill date, added 2026-08-29.** Without it `flush.py` always writes
to *today's* log, so recovering old stranded files silently misfiles them under the current
date. Always pass the date parsed from the filename when backfilling; entries are then
marked `(backfilled …)`.

**Batch-recovery trap — the 60-second dedup guard destroys data.** `flush.py` skips a run
whose `sessio…

…n have several stranded files (different timestamps), so
a loop that hits the same uuid twice inside a minute silently loses the second one — it still
prints as consumed. Hit 2026-08-29: 12 files ran, 10 flushed, 2 dropped. Before trusting a

11	When memsearch fails to open `~/.memsearch/milvus.db`, milvus-lite prints:
12	
13	> Failed to open the local Milvus Lite database. If this database was created with an older Milvus Lite release, it may not be compatible with Milvus Lite 3.x. Move the existing .db file aside, then rebuild the index...
14	
15	**That text is a generic open-failure string, not a version verdict.** It fires just as readily on plain lock contention. Diagnosed 2026-08-14: the underlying error was `BlockingIOError: [Errno 35]` from `flock`, and `lsof +D ~/.memsearch/milvus.db` named the holder — a concurrent manual `memsearch index` running after the SecondBrain vault move. The same DB with the same milvus-lite 3.1.1 had indexed successfully hours earlier.
16	
17	(Attribution caution: at the time this was written the holder was assumed to be "another Claude session," inferred from an unfamiliar PID and shell-snapshot id. Eric corrected that — it was not. `lsof` tells you *which process*, never *which agent or person*; state the process and leave the actor unnamed.)
18	
19	**Why:** following the message's advice (move the .db aside, rebuild) throws away a working index and costs an hours-scale re-index of the SecondBrain library — a self-inflicted outage in response to a transient collision.
20	
21	**How to apply:**
22	- Before believing any milvus-lite "incompatible database" message, run `lsof +D ~/.memsearch/milvus.db` and `ps aux | grep memsearch`. A live holder means wait, not rebuild.
23	- Milvus Lite is single-writer. `daily-backup.ps1`'s advisory lock (`.memsearch-index.lock`, ~line 416) coordinates the nightly reindex with the SessionEnd hook only — it cannot see a hand-run `memsearch index`, so manual indexing during a backup window collides. Avoid running `memsearch index` by hand while the nightly backup may fire.
24	- `memsearch-index:full-set` in `.errors.log` is therefore usually transient. Confirm the lock is free, then let the next scheduled run clear it.
25	
26	**Tooling mitigation added 2026-08-14 (because the written warning was not enough).** Later the same day a session ran `memsearch reset --yes` anyway and triggered a ~2h full rebuild — the exact outage this note warns about, with the note already on disk. Prose guidance does not survive contact with a scary error message, so the guard is now in code:
27	
28	- `~/.local/bin/ms-search` — lock-aware retry wrapper for reads (`search` / `stats` / `expand` / `transcript`; write subcommands are refused). Retries with backoff to 60s (`MS_SEARCH_MAX_WAIT`), then exits **75** saying the DB is healthy and not to run `reset`. It retries **only** on `DataDirLockedError` / `another process holds the lock` / `Resource temporarily unavailable` / `_acquire_lock` / `fcntl.flock`; it deliberately does **not** key on the "may not be compatible with Milvus Lite 3.x" sentence, since that same wording is emitted for genuine incompatibility — so real corruption still fails fast and passes its exit code through.

Caveat: `bumpTransientStreak` shares one counter across all transient classes at threshold 6, so a cluster of session-ends during a long rebuild can still escalate — downgraded, not eliminated.
30	
31	**How to apply (updated):** prefer `ms-search "query"` over `memsearch search` for recall; it waits out a busy index instead of surfacing the misleading message. Reserve bare `memsearch` for writes.
32

- `~/.local/bin/ms-search` — lock-aware retry wrapper for reads (`search` / `stats` / `expand` / `transcript`; write subcommands are refused). Retries with backoff to 60s (`MS_SEARCH_MAX_WAIT`), then exits **75** saying the DB is healthy and not to run `reset`. It retries **only** on `DataDirLockedError` / `another process holds the lock` / `Resource temporarily unavailable` / `_acquire_lock` / `fcntl.flock`; it deliberately does **not** key on the "may not be compatible with Milvus Lite 3.x" sentence, since that same wording is emitted for genuine incompatibility — so real corruption still fails fast and passes its exit code through.
- `~/.claude/hooks/memsearch-sync.js` now classifies those same lock signatures as transient instead of escalating them as hard errors. Caveat: `bumpTransientStreak` shares one counter across all transient classes at threshold 6, so a cluster of session-ends during a long rebuild can still escalate — downgraded, not eliminated.

**How to apply (updated):** prefer `ms-search "query"` over `memsearch search` for recall; it waits out a busy index instead of surfacing the misleading message. Reserve bare `memsearch` for writes.

4	metadata:

10	
11	The compiler at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/` has three stages. Each fails
12	differently and the symptoms look alike, so identify the stage before fixing.
13	
14	**Stage 1 — `hooks/session-end.py`.** Writes `scripts/session-flush-<uuid>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMMSS>.md`,
15	then spawns `flush.py`. Logs every firing to `scripts/flush.log` as `SessionEnd fired`.
16	If `flush.log` has no such line for days but the hook works when run by hand, sessions
17	are being *closed* rather than exited cleanly — not a config break. Self-verifying: end
18	one session normally and re-check the tail.
19	
20	**Stage 2 — `scripts/flush.py`.** Calls the Agent SDK, appends to `daily/<date>.md`, writes
21	`scripts/last-flush.json` **only on success**, and **deletes its context file on success**.
22	Therefore **every leftover `session-flush-*.md` is a flush that died**, and its datestamp
23	maps to a missing `daily/<date>.md`. That is the cheapest diagnostic in the whole system —
24	count the leftovers. A stale `last-flush.json` means flushes are *dying*, not that the hook
25	never fired. Recover one by hand:
26	`uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/flush.py <context-file> <session-id> [YYYY-MM-DD]`
27	Success = `Result: FLUSH_OK` + `Flush complete` in `flush.log`.
28	
29	**The third arg is a backfill date, added 2026-08-29.** Without it `flush.py` always writes
30	to *today's* log, so recovering old stranded files silently misfiles them under the current
31	date. Always pass the date parsed from the filename when backfilling; entries are then
32	marked `(backfilled …)`.
33	
34	**Batch-recovery trap — the 60-second dedup guard destroys data.** `flush.py` skips a run
35	whose `session_id` matches `last-flush.json` within 60s, and **deletes the context file on
36	that skip path too**. One session can have several stranded files (different timestamps), so
37	a loop that hits the same uuid twice inside a minute silently loses the second one — it still
38	prints as consumed. Hit 2026-08-29: 12 files ran, 10 flushed, 2 dropped. Before trusting a
39	batch, check `grep -c "Skipping duplicate flush" flush.log`, and either group runs so repeats
40	of a uuid are >60s apart or run repeats individually.
41	Recovery is possible because `~/.claude` is captured to the SSD: the deleted files came back
42	from `/Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup/claude/claude-memory-compiler/scripts/`.
43	
44	**Stage 3 — memsearch index.** `INDEX full set: Indexed 0 chunks` in the nightly log is
45	**usually not an indexer fault** — it means nothing new arrived. A dead stage 2 starves it
46	and looks identical. Check leftovers/`last-flush.json` before suspecting memsearch.
47	memsearch is a **uv tool**: binary `~/.local/bin/memsearch`, env
48	`~/.local/share/uv/tools/memsearch/`. Test an import directly with that env's python
49	(`.../memsearch/bin/python -c "import onnxruntime"`) rather than inferring from index counts.
50	Reinstall with `uv tool install --force memsearch`, never pip — and re-apply the local flush
51	patch afterwards, which any reinstall strips.
52	
53	**`hooks/session-start.py` — rewritten 2026-08-29.** It used to paste all of
54	`knowledge/index.md` into every session. That file is ~48k chars against a 20k cap, so the
55	index was truncated mid-table **and the `## Recent Daily Log` section was pushed off the end
56	entirely** — the one part that is always relevant never arrived. It now emits a pointer
57	(article counts + paths + the `memsearch search` command) and always includes the log:
58	20,039 → 682 chars. If a session needs the index, read
59	`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/knowledge/index.md` on demand. Backups of the pre-change
60	files are `*.bak-2026-08-29` beside each.

#!/bin/bash
# brain-audit measurement pass. Facts only, no judgement.
# Emits `key: value` lines. The skill scores from these; it must not guess them.
# Deliberately never fails the whole run: a missing path prints "MISSING", not an error.

VAULT="/Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain"
CLAUDE_DIR="/Users/kristinarash/.claude"
TIER_A="$CLAUDE_DIR/projects/-Users-kristinarash-DEV/memory"
TODAY=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)

# newest mtime (YYYY-MM-DD) of *.md under a dir; "none" if empty/missing
newest() {
  [ -d "$1" ] || { echo "none"; return; }
  # `{} +` batches the stat calls. `{} \;` spawns one process per file and made
  # a full run take minutes once the vault passed ~800 notes.
  find "$1" -name '*.md' -exec stat -f '%Sm' -t '%Y-%m-%d' {} + 2>/dev/null | sort -r | head -1 | grep . || echo "none"
}
count() {
  [ -d "$1" ] || { echo 0; return; }
  find "$1" -name '*.md' 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' '
}
# whole days between YYYY-MM-DD and today.
# Both timestamps are pinned to 12:00:00. BSD `date -j -f '%Y-%m-%d'` fills the
# unspecified time fields from the clock at call time, so two calls in the same
# run drifted and the same date reported 34 days in one line and 35 in the next.
days_since() {
  [ "$1" = "none" ] && { echo "-"; return; }
  local t s
  t=$(date -j -f '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' "$TODAY 12:00:00" +%s 2>/dev/null) || { echo "-"; return; }
  s=$(date -j -f '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' "$1 12:00:00" +%s 2>/dev/null) || { echo "-"; return; }
  echo $(( (t - s) / 86400 ))
}

echo "run_date: $TODAY"
echo ""

echo "## vault folders (count | newest | days_stale)"
for d in Notes Drafts Archive Knowledge Projects Inbox; do
  n=$(newest "$VAULT/$d")
  echo "$d: $(count "$VAULT/$d") | $n | $(days_since "$n")"

## The 6 shifts (the principles part 2 audits against)

| # | Then | Now | The principle |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Give Claude rules | Let Claude use judgement | constrain Claude only where a wrong call is genuinely costly; judgement covers the rest |
| 2 | Give Claude examples | Design interfaces | a well-designed parameter, name, or field teaches use better than worked examples |
| 3 | Put it all upfront | Use progressive disclosure | the right context at the right time; always-loaded files must earn every line |
| 4 | Repeat yourself | Simple tool descriptions | every instruction has one authoritative home; everything else points there |
| 5 | Memory in CLAUDE.md | Auto-memory | facts about the user and the work belong in the memory system, not guidance files |
| 6 | Simple specs | Rich references | the highest-fidelity reference wins: code, test suites, HTML mockups, rubrics |

## Workflow

### Part 1 - the standard checkup
1. Run `claude doctor` via Bash with a 60s timeout. If it completes, summarize its findings.
2. If it hangs or needs an interactive screen, note "run /doctor in your session for the built-in half" and move on. Never block on it.

### Part 2 - the 6 shift checks
Scope: whatever the workspace actually loads as context - guidance files (CLAUDE.md and kin), skills, rules, memory indexes. Map that set first; don't assume the workspace's layout. Always exclude ver

**Audit the principles, not surface patterns.** This audit itself follows shift 1: judge each file against the principle, don't pattern-match for keywords. Read the context the way Claude receives it 

1. **Judgement over rules** - is Claude constrained where judgement would serve better? Smell: absolute directives about matters of taste or style, or two directives that pull against each other. Safe
2. **Interfaces over examples** - do skills teach by boxing Claude into worked examples where a clearer interface (better parameters, names, structure) would carry it?
3. **Progressive disclosure over upfront loading** - does every always-loaded line earn its place? Smell: detail that's only occasionally needed sitting in files that load every session instead of a t
4. **One home over repetition** - does each instruction have one authoritative home? Smell: the same guidance restated in several places, especially copies that have drifted apart.
5. **Auto-memory over guidance-file memory** - are facts about the user or the work (preferences, dates, decisions) living as prose in guidance files instead of the memory system?

# Improve System — Vault Audit

Find rot in the vault and report it. Verification only: this skill proposes, the user disposes.

## Step 0 — read the pending ledger first

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/reports/proposals-pending.md`

Do this **before** scanning. Apply anything marked `approved` (then mark it `applied`),
and re-list every `open` item in this run's report next to the new findings. Append new
findings there as `open`, deduplicating against what is already listed.

Without this step a proposal made in a session that ends is lost, and the next run pays
to rediscover it. The file's header carries the entry format.

**Vault:** `vault_root` in the selected platform config
**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.

Scan `Notes/`, `Knowledge/`, `Projects/` (skip `Archive/`, `Inbox/`, `morning-briefings/`).

1. **Stale**: `status: seed` notes older than 60 days; `Project_*.md` files untouched 30+ days that read as active.
2. **Conflicting**: notes asserting opposing claims on the same domain/tags — compare titles and opening claims, read bodies only for suspected pairs.
3. **Duplicates**: near-identical titles or same core concept under different slugs.

Output a short report grouped by issue type with a proposed action per item (merge / archive / update status / no action). **Apply nothing until the user picks.** Archive = move to `Archive/`, never d

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the Windows-machine slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

## Daily compiled logs — read-only

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never hand-edit these files.** The compiler owns them.
- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## What is loaded at session start

`~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are read once at session start and are a **frozen snapshot**. Mid-session writes persist to disk but only take effect next session — this is deliberate, to preserve the prefix cache. Never load more than the

# unspecified time fields from the clock at call time, so two calls in the same
# run drifted and the same date reported 34 days in one line and 35 in the next.
days_since() {
  [ "$1" = "none" ] && { echo "-"; return; }
  local t s
  t=$(date -j -f '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' "$TODAY 12:00:00" +%s 2>/dev/null) || { echo "-"; return; }
  s=$(date -j -f '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' "$1 12:00:00" +%s 2>/dev/null) || { echo "-"; return; }
  echo $(( (t - s) / 86400 ))
}

for d in Notes Drafts Archive Knowledge Projects Inbox; do
  n=$(newest "$VAULT/$d")
  echo "$d: $(count "$VAULT/$d") | $n | $(days_since "$n")"

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/reports/proposals-pending.md`

findings there as `open`, deduplicating against what is already listed.

Without this step a proposal made in a session that ends is lost, and the next run pays

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the Windows-machine slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

const HOME='C:/Users/eric_rash'; const cutoff=Date.now()-30*864e5; const root=HOME+'/.claude/projects';
let files=[]; for(const s of fs.readdirSync(root)){const d=path.join(root,s); let st; try{st=fs.statSync(d)}catch{continue} if(!st.isDirectory())continue; for(const f of fs.readdirSync(d)){ if(!f.endsWith('.jsonl'))continue; const p=path.join(d,f); if(fs.statSync(p).mtimeMs>=cutoff) files.push({p,slug:s});} }
const qs=[]; 
(async()=>{
for(const {p,slug} of files){
  const rl=readline.createInterface({input:fs.createReadStream(p,{encoding:'utf8'}),crlfDelay:Infinity});
  for await(const line of rl){
    if(!line.includes('memsearch search')||!line.includes('"tool_use"'))continue;
    let j; try{j=JSON.parse(line)}catch{continue}
    const c=j.message&&j.message.content; if(!Array.isArray(c))continue;
    for(const b of c){ if(b.type!=='tool_use')continue; const cmd=(b.input&&b.input.command)||''; const re=/memsearch\s+search\s+(?:"([^"]+)"|'([^']+)'|(\S+))/g; let m; while((m=re.exec(cmd))){ qs.push({q:(m[1]||m[2]||m[3]).slice(0,110), mac:slug.startsWith('-Users'), date:(j.timestamp||'').slice(0,10)}); } }
  }
}
console.log('queries found:',qs.length,'| from Mac slugs:',qs.filter(x=>x.mac).length,'Windows slugs:',qs.filter(x=>!x.mac).length);
const uniq=[...new Map(qs.map(x=>[x.q.toLowerCase(),x])).values()];
console.log('unique:',uniq.length);
uniq.forEach(x=>console.log(`${x.date} ${x.mac?'mac':'win'} :: ${x.q}`));
})();
```

# Memory & automation infrastructure audit — 2026-09-30 (Windows laptop)

tagged **[M]** measured this session on this machine, or **[I]** inferred from notes,
code comments, or reasoning. Mac-side state is [I] throughout (not inspectable from here).

Scope: is the Docker/Milvus vector stack still worth running for memory recall now that
the working models carry 1M-token context, and how should the memory stack be evaluated
repeatably rather than by opinion.

---

## 1. Verdict in three lines

1. **Retire Docker/Milvus on Windows.** It exists only because `milvus-lite` ships no
   Windows wheel (memsearch's own `store.py` says so [M]). It costs ~1.7 GB of resident RAM,
   6.6 GB of disk, one more daemon that has to be up before any session ends, and it is not
   where memsearch's latency goes. A stdlib SQLite FTS5 index over the same markdown matched
   memsearch 9/10 vs 10/10 on a 10-question pilot at <10 ms vs 4.4 s per query [M].
2. **The bigger recall problem on this machine is not the backend, it is coverage.** Three
   of the 12 configured index paths point at `~/SecondBrain/...`, which does not exist on
   Windows (the vault is `~/Desktop/SecondBrain`). The hook filters missing paths silently,
   so the 1,370-note vault (~1.6M tokens) is not indexed here [M]. Real queries from 09-27
   ("Zatsiorsky", "Issurin") had 53 and 57 matching vault notes but memsearch's top hit was
   `dev-docs/Flint/QUEUE.md` [M]. Fix this regardless of backend.
3. **Evaluate, don't opine.** A 53-query seed set already exists in the transcripts (the
   actual `memsearch search` strings from the last 30 days, listed in Appendix A). Label
   expected answers for ~20 of them, run the runner in section 6 against memsearch / rg /
   FTS5 on both machines, and fold it into `claude-stack-doctor`'s weekly run.

---

## 2. What the stack is (sizes)

| 2 | where renv libraries live on Windows | transcripts/2026-09-22 | HIT 4.0 s | HIT | HIT |
| 3 | live OKR doc for the status report | project_status-report-sourcing | HIT 3.7 s | HIT | miss |

| 9 | department names never to use | user_baylor-department-names | HIT 4.2 s | miss (54 files match "S&C") | HIT |

- **Bias:** 9/10 expected files are Tier A notes whose titles already sit in the injected

## 5. Docker/Milvus: recommendation, migration, rollback

### 5.1 Verdict

Retire the Docker/Milvus stack on Windows and move memory recall to SQLite FTS5 (no
server, stdlib Python, identical on both machines). Keep the vector option as an
*evaluated* upgrade, not a default: if the seed-set eval ever shows FTS5 losing by more
than one hit@5 on n≥30, add embeddings back via `sqlite-vec` (embedded, Windows-capable)
with the same ONNX model — that restores semantics without the daemon, but also restores
the 3–5 s embedder cost.

Why now and not before: with 1M context and stronger models, the retrieval layer's job
shrank to "find the right 3–5 files", after which the model reads them whole. Chunk-level
semantic precision mattered when the budget was 200k and the model needed the exact
paragraph; it matters much less when reading five whole notes costs 10k tokens.

### 5.2 Recommended replacement path (one code path on both machines)

Two viable shapes. Prefer **A**; **B** is the zero-build alternative.

**A. `mem` — a ~150-line stdlib script (`~/.claude/scripts/mem.py`, wrapped as `mem`).**
- `mem index` — walks the same `memory-index-paths.json` (with a `{VAULT}` token resolved
  from `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`), splits markdown by heading,
  upserts into `~/.claude/mem-fts.db` (FTS5, `porter unicode61`, content hash per section,
  file mtime skip). Full build ≈ 17 s for 11.8 MB in memory [M]; incremental is sub-second.
- `mem search "q" --top-k 5` — BM25 with phrase boost, prints memsearch's `Source:` /
  `Heading:` / snippet layout so `memory-write`, `session-miner`, and `stack-check.ps1` keep
  working with a one-word substitution.
- `mem stats`, `mem coverage` (prints each configured root as EXISTS/MISSING — the check
  that would have caught the vault gap).
- No embeddings, no model cache needed, no Docker, no lock (SQLite handles concurrent
  readers; single writer via the existing PID lock in the hook).

**B. context-mode `ctx_index` over the same roots.** Already installed, already FTS5 with a
better ranker, already the model's most-used recall tool (448 calls/30 d). Downsides: MCP-
only (Codex hooks and PowerShell scripts cannot call it), project-scoped store, and its
content DB is already 70 MB of session captures. Fine as the *interactive* path; A is
still needed for scripts and Codex.

Both machines: A runs identically on macOS and Windows (Python 3 stdlib). The Mac's Milvus
Lite can stay as an untouched fallback since it costs nothing while idle [I], but the
two-copies trap says run the *same* retriever on both, so switch the Mac once the Windows
eval holds for ~30 days.

### 5.3 Migration steps (ordered; nothing destructive until step 7)

0. **Prerequisite, both machines:** add `{VAULT}` to `memory-index-paths.json`, resolve it
   from `_shared/config.<platform>.json` in `memsearch-sync.js` and `daily-backup.ps1`, add
   the Windows DEV slug, and make the hook **log every skipped path** to `.errors.log`. Do
   this even if nothing else changes.
1. Write `mem.py` + `mem` wrapper; `mem index`; run the section-6 eval against memsearch,
   rg, and `mem` on the seed set. Record the result file.
2. Point `memory-write` L1 at `mem search` (keep `memsearch search` as L1b on Mac for now);
   update `session-miner`, `closeout`, `dev-sync`, `harvest`, `backup`, `meeting-prep`,
   `ingest-book`, `library-*` SKILL.md mentions (13 skill files + 13 `~/.codex/skills` copies
   [M], 51 files total mention memsearch — grep list in Appendix B).
3. `memsearch-sync.js` worker: call `mem index` instead of `memsearch index` (seconds, no
   RAM spike, no 600 s cap needed). Same for `KeystoneOS/scripts/codex-hooks/memsearch-sync.ps1`
   and `daily-backup.ps1`'s index step.
4. Disable `\Eric\memsearch-drain-once` and `memsearch-drain-weekly` scheduled tasks.
5. Replace the `memsearch search "healthcheck"` + `docker ps` block in `stack-check.ps1`
   with `mem coverage` + a 5-question eval subset.
6. `docker compose -f ~/.memsearch/milvus/docker-compose.yml stop` (not `down`); turn off
   Docker Desktop AutoStart. Reclaims ~1.7 GB RAM and removes the "Docker must be up before
   any session ends" dependency. Leave images/volumes for 30 days.
7. After 30 clean days and one passing eval: `docker compose down -v`, `docker image prune`,
   optionally uninstall Docker Desktop (unless memsearch/Milvus is needed for something else
   — nothing else on this machine uses Docker [M: only distro is docker-desktop; Ubuntu is
   stopped]).
8. Mac: repeat 1–3 with the same script; leave `milvus.db` in place as fallback.

### 5.4 Rollback

- `config.toml` is untouched throughout. `docker compose up -d` from the same compose file
  restores the stack; re-enable AutoStart; restore the three hook lines from the `.bak`

- `questions.jsonl` — one line per case:

  Seed with Appendix A (53 real queries) + the 10 pilot cases. Labelling rule: the
  expected file is the one the *session that asked* ended up reading or citing — pull it
  from the same transcript. Budget: ~30 min to label 20; grow by 5 per month from new
  sessions (the extraction script in 6.2 prints candidates).
- `recall-eval.py` — stdlib only. Backends: `memsearch`, `mem` (FTS5), `rg` (uses the
  `keyword` field), optionally `ctx` (via a tiny MCP client, or skip). Per case it records
  rank of first expected file, latency, chars returned, exit status/timeout, and
  **coverage** (does any expected file exist under the configured roots on *this* machine —
  the check that exposes path drift).

  sessions, `memsearch`/`mem`/rg/`ctx_search` call counts, hook error lines, flush

### 6.2 Metrics and decision rule

- **hit@5** (primary), hit@1, MRR; **p50/p95 latency**; **failure rate** (non-zero exit,
  timeout, backend unreachable); **coverage** (expected file reachable by the index on this
  machine); **chars returned** as the token-cost proxy.
- Retire or demote a retrieval layer when the cheaper one is within **1 hit@5 on n≥30** and
  beats it on failure rate and latency for **two consecutive runs**. Reinstate embeddings
  only if FTS5 falls >1 hit@5 behind on the same rule.
- Report per-layer, not just overall: a backend can be perfect on Tier A and useless on
  transcripts.

### 6.3 When to rerun

- Any model change in `settings.json` (`model`, `advisorModel`) or a Claude Code major.
- Any memsearch / context-mode / `mem.py` upgrade; any edit to `memory-index-paths.json`.
- Monthly via `claude-stack-doctor`'s existing `weekly-check.ps1` (run the 5-case smoke
  subset weekly, full set monthly); on both machines, so the ledger shows drift between them.

Fold into **`claude-stack-doctor`**, not the others: it already owns the memsearch smoke
test, the weekly scheduled run, the cross-machine handoff check, and the `.errors.log`
read. `doctor-plus` audits guidance-file principles, `brain-audit` scores the vault,
`improve-system` finds vault rot — none of them measure retrieval. Add two findings codes to
`stack-check.ps1`: `recall-coverage` (any configured root MISSING) and `recall-regress`
(hit@5 dropped ≥2 vs last ledger row).

Read-only investigation. Nothing edited, stopped, or reconfigured. Every number is
tagged **[M]** measured this session on this machine, or **[I]** inferred from notes,
code comments, or reasoning. Mac-side state is [I] throughout (not inspectable from here).

Scope: is the Docker/Milvus vector stack still worth running for memory recall now that
the working models carry 1M-token context, and how should the memory stack be evaluated
repeatably rather than by opinion.

## 1. Verdict in three lines

1. **Retire Docker/Milvus on Windows.** It exists only because `milvus-lite` ships no
   Windows wheel (memsearch's own `store.py` says so [M]). It costs ~1.7 GB of resident RAM,
   6.6 GB of disk, one more daemon that has to be up before any session ends, and it is not
   where memsearch's latency goes. A stdlib SQLite FTS5 index over the same markdown matched
   memsearch 9/10 vs 10/10 on a 10-question pilot at <10 ms vs 4.4 s per query [M].
2. **The bigger recall problem on this machine is not the backend, it is coverage.** Three
   of the 12 configured index paths point at `~/SecondBrain/...`, which does not exist on
   Windows (the vault is `~/Desktop/SecondBrain`). The hook filters missing paths silently,
   so the 1,370-note vault (~1.6M tokens) is not indexed here [M]. Real queries from 09-27
   ("Zatsiorsky", "Issurin") had 53 and 57 matching vault notes but memsearch's top hit was
   `dev-docs/Flint/QUEUE.md` [M]. Fix this regardless of backend.
3. **Evaluate, don't opine.** A 53-query seed set already exists in the transcripts (the
   actual `memsearch search` strings from the last 30 days, listed in Appendix A). Label
   expected answers for ~20 of them, run the runner in section 6 against memsearch / rg /
   FTS5 on both machines, and fold it into `claude-stack-doctor`'s weekly run.

- FTS5 was Python's stdlib `sqlite3` with `porter unicode61` and a naive OR query — no
  tuning, no trigram, no phrase boosting. context-mode's FTS5 (stemming + trigram + RRF +
  proximity rerank) is a stronger keyword engine and is already installed and used 448×/30 d.

### 4.1 Real-query coverage check [M]

For 10 of the real 09-27 Windows queries: files matching in the reachable index vs in the
unindexed vault, and what memsearch actually returned.

| Real query | matches in indexed roots | matches in vault (unindexed) | memsearch top-1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zatsiorsky | 8 | **53** | dev-docs/Flint/QUEUE.md |
| Issurin block periodization | 10 | **57** | dev-docs/Flint/QUEUE.md |
| stretching matrix system | 1 | 3 | dev-docs/FaceComps/fall-camp/… |
| Omegawave sympathetic parasympathetic | 1 | 5 | dev-docs/…EOS_Football_Analys… |
| Gallucci research project approval | 9 | 18 | dev-docs/BAIR_Steering_Committee/… |
| kitman labs AMS | 51 | 36 | knowledge/concepts/at-utilization… |

| perch duckdb owner | 88 | 29 | dev-docs/_INBOX/STATUS.md |

Five of ten real questions had most of their answers in the corpus that is not indexed on
this machine, and the vector search confidently returned queue/status files instead.
No backend fixes that; the path config does.

---

## 5. Docker/Milvus: recommendation, migration, rollback

### 5.1 Verdict

Retire the Docker/Milvus stack on Windows and move memory recall to SQLite FTS5 (no
server, stdlib Python, identical on both machines). Keep the vector option as an
*evaluated* upgrade, not a default: if the seed-set eval ever shows FTS5 losing by more
than one hit@5 on n≥30, add embeddings back via `sqlite-vec` (embedded, Windows-capable)
with the same ONNX model — that restores semantics without the daemon, but also restores
the 3–5 s embedder cost.

Why now and not before: with 1M context and stronger models, the retrieval layer's job
shrank to "find the right 3–5 files", after which the model reads them whole. Chunk-level
semantic precision mattered when the budget was 200k and the model needed the exact
paragraph; it matters much less when reading five whole notes costs 10k tokens.

### 5.2 Recommended replacement path (one code path on both machines)

Two viable shapes. Prefer **A**; **B** is the zero-build alternative.

**A. `mem` — a ~150-line stdlib script (`~/.claude/scripts/mem.py`, wrapped as `mem`).**
- `mem index` — walks the same `memory-index-paths.json` (with a `{VAULT}` token resolved
  from `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`), splits markdown by heading,
  upserts into `~/.claude/mem-fts.db` (FTS5, `porter unicode61`, content hash per section,
  file mtime skip). Full build ≈ 17 s for 11.8 MB in memory [M]; incremental is sub-second.
- `mem search "q" --top-k 5` — BM25 with phrase boost, prints memsearch's `Source:` /
  `Heading:` / snippet layout so `memory-write`, `session-miner`, and `stack-check.ps1` keep
  working with a one-word substitution.
- `mem stats`, `mem coverage` (prints each configured root as EXISTS/MISSING — the check
  that would have caught the vault gap).
- No embeddings, no model cache needed, no Docker, no lock (SQLite handles concurrent
  readers; single writer via the existing PID lock in the hook).

**B. context-mode `ctx_index` over the same roots.** Already installed, already FTS5 with a
better ranker, already the model's most-used recall tool (448 calls/30 d). Downsides: MCP-
only (Codex hooks and PowerShell scripts cannot call it), project-scoped store, and its
content DB is already 70 MB of session captures. Fine as the *interactive* path; A is
still needed for scripts and Codex.

Both machines: A runs identically on macOS and Windows (Python 3 stdlib). The Mac's Milvus
Lite can stay as an untouched fallback since it costs nothing while idle [I], but the
two-copies trap says run the *same* retriever on both, so switch the Mac once the Windows
eval holds for ~30 days.

### 5.3 Migration steps (ordered; nothing destructive until step 7)

0. **Prerequisite, both machines:** add `{VAULT}` to `memory-index-paths.json`, resolve it
   from `_shared/config.<platform>.json` in `memsearch-sync.js` and `daily-backup.ps1`, add
   the Windows DEV slug, and make the hook **log every skipped path** to `.errors.log`. Do
   this even if nothing else changes.
1. Write `mem.py` + `mem` wrapper; `mem index`; run the section-6 eval against memsearch,
   rg, and `mem` on the seed set. Record the result file.
2. Point `memory-write` L1 at `mem search` (keep `memsearch search` as L1b on Mac for now);
   update `session-miner`, `closeout`, `dev-sync`, `harvest`, `backup`, `meeting-prep`,
   `ingest-book`, `library-*` SKILL.md mentions (13 skill files + 13 `~/.codex/skills` copies
   [M], 51 files total mention memsearch — grep list in Appendix B).
3. `memsearch-sync.js` worker: call `mem index` instead of `memsearch index` (seconds, no
   RAM spike, no 600 s cap needed). Same for `KeystoneOS/scripts/codex-hooks/memsearch-sync.ps1`
   and `daily-backup.ps1`'s index step.
4. Disable `\Eric\memsearch-drain-once` and `memsearch-drain-weekly` scheduled tasks.
5. Replace the `memsearch search "healthcheck"` + `docker ps` block in `stack-check.ps1`
   with `mem coverage` + a 5-question eval subset.
6. `docker compose -f ~/.memsearch/milvus/docker-compose.yml stop` (not `down`); turn off
   Docker Desktop AutoStart. Reclaims ~1.7 GB RAM and removes the "Docker must be up before
   any session ends" dependency. Leave images/volumes for 30 days.
7. After 30 clean days and one passing eval: `docker compose down -v`, `docker image prune`,
   optionally uninstall Docker Desktop (unless memsearch/Milvus is needed for something else
   — nothing else on this machine uses Docker [M: only distro is docker-desktop; Ubuntu is
   stopped]).
8. Mac: repeat 1–3 with the same script; leave `milvus.db` in place as fallback.

### 5.4 Rollback

- `config.toml` is untouched throughout. `docker compose up -d` from the same compose file
  restores the stack; re-enable AutoStart; restore the three hook lines from the `.bak`
  files the hooks already keep. The Milvus index survives in the volumes until step 7.
- If volumes were pruned: `Start-ScheduledTask -TaskPath '\Eric\' -TaskName memsearch-drain-weekly`
  rebuilds; measured 232 min for 8,764 chunks, so budget ~8 h for the full 18k [I: scaled].
- Skills keep working during rollback because `mem search` and `memsearch search` share an
  output format.

---

## 6. Repeatable evaluation method

Goal: a number, not a feeling, every time a model or a retrieval component changes.

### 6.1 Artifacts (all under `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/`, git-synced with the memory repo)

- `questions.jsonl` — one line per case:
  `{"id","query","keyword","expected":[basename…],"layer":"tierA|daily|transcript|vault|dev-docs","source_session","added","machine"}`.
  Seed with Appendix A (53 real queries) + the 10 pilot cases. Labelling rule: the
  expected file is the one the *session that asked* ended up reading or citing — pull it
  from the same transcript. Budget: ~30 min to label 20; grow by 5 per month from new
  sessions (the extraction script in 6.2 prints candidates).
- `recall-eval.py` — stdlib only. Backends: `memsearch`, `mem` (FTS5), `rg` (uses the
  `keyword` field), optionally `ctx` (via a tiny MCP client, or skip). Per case it records
  rank of first expected file, latency, chars returned, exit status/timeout, and
  **coverage** (does any expected file exist under the configured roots on *this* machine —
  the check that exposes path drift).
- `telemetry.py` — the 30-day transcript scan used in this audit: human vs headless
  sessions, `memsearch`/`mem`/rg/`ctx_search` call counts, hook error lines, flush
  outcomes. Cheap (streams 683 MB in ~2 min [M]).
- `results/<date>-<machine>-<model>.json` + one appended row in `ledger.md`:
  `date | machine | model | backend | n | hit@1 | hit@5 | MRR | p50 ms | p95 ms | fail% | coverage%`.

### 6.2 Metrics and decision rule

- **hit@5** (primary), hit@1, MRR; **p50/p95 latency**; **failure rate** (non-zero exit,
  timeout, backend unreachable); **coverage** (expected file reachable by the index on this
  machine); **chars returned** as the token-cost proxy.
- Retire or demote a retrieval layer when the cheaper one is within **1 hit@5 on n≥30** and
  beats it on failure rate and latency for **two consecutive runs**. Reinstate embeddings
  only if FTS5 falls >1 hit@5 behind on the same rule.
- Report per-layer, not just overall: a backend can be perfect on Tier A and useless on
  transcripts.

### 6.3 When to rerun

- Any model change in `settings.json` (`model`, `advisorModel`) or a Claude Code major.
- Any memsearch / context-mode / `mem.py` upgrade; any edit to `memory-index-paths.json`.
- Monthly via `claude-stack-doctor`'s existing `weekly-check.ps1` (run the 5-case smoke
  subset weekly, full set monthly); on both machines, so the ledger shows drift between them.

### 6.4 Where it lives

Fold into **`claude-stack-doctor`**, not the others: it already owns the memsearch smoke
test, the weekly scheduled run, the cross-machine handoff check, and the `.errors.log`
read. `doctor-plus` audits guidance-file principles, `brain-audit` scores the vault,
`improve-system` finds vault rot — none of them measure retrieval. Add two findings codes to
`stack-check.ps1`: `recall-coverage` (any configured root MISSING) and `recall-regress`
(hit@5 dropped ≥2 vs last ledger row).

---

## 5. Docker/Milvus: recommendation, migration, rollback

### 5.1 Verdict

Retire the Docker/Milvus stack on Windows and move memory recall to SQLite FTS5 (no
server, stdlib Python, identical on both machines). Keep the vector option as an
*evaluated* upgrade, not a default: if the seed-set eval ever shows FTS5 losing by more
than one hit@5 on n≥30, add embeddings back via `sqlite-vec` (embedded, Windows-capable)
with the same ONNX model — that restores semantics without the daemon, but also restores
the 3–5 s embedder cost.

Why now and not before: with 1M context and stronger models, the retrieval layer's job
shrank to "find the right 3–5 files", after which the model reads them whole. Chunk-level
semantic precision mattered when the budget was 200k and the model needed the exact
paragraph; it matters much less when reading five whole notes costs 10k tokens.

### 5.2 Recommended replacement path (one code path on both machines)

Two viable shapes. Prefer **A**; **B** is the zero-build alternative.

**A. `mem` — a ~150-line stdlib script (`~/.claude/scripts/mem.py`, wrapped as `mem`).**
- `mem index` — walks the same `memory-index-paths.json` (with a `{VAULT}` token resolved
  from `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`), splits markdown by heading,
  upserts into `~/.claude/mem-fts.db` (FTS5, `porter unicode61`, content hash per section,
  file mtime skip). Full build ≈ 17 s for 11.8 MB in memory [M]; incremental is sub-second.
- `mem search "q" --top-k 5` — BM25 with phrase boost, prints memsearch's `Source:` /
  `Heading:` / snippet layout so `memory-write`, `session-miner`, and `stack-check.ps1` keep
  working with a one-word substitution.
- `mem stats`, `mem coverage` (prints each configured root as EXISTS/MISSING — the check
  that would have caught the vault gap).
- No embeddings, no model cache needed, no Docker, no lock (SQLite handles concurrent
  readers; single writer via the existing PID lock in the hook).

**B. context-mode `ctx_index` over the same roots.** Already installed, already FTS5 with a
better ranker, already the model's most-used recall tool (448 calls/30 d). Downsides: MCP-
only (Codex hooks and PowerShell scripts cannot call it), project-scoped store, and its
content DB is already 70 MB of session captures. Fine as the *interactive* path; A is
still needed for scripts and Codex.

Both machines: A runs identically on macOS and Windows (Python 3 stdlib). The Mac's Milvus
Lite can stay as an untouched fallback since it costs nothing while idle [I], but the
two-copies trap says run the *same* retriever on both, so switch the Mac once the Windows
eval holds for ~30 days.

### 5.3 Migration steps (ordered; nothing destructive until step 7)

0. **Prerequisite, both machines:** add `{VAULT}` to `memory-index-paths.json`, resolve it
   from `_shared/config.<platform>.json` in `memsearch-sync.js` and `daily-backup.ps1`, add
   the Windows DEV slug, and make the hook **log every skipped path** to `.errors.log`. Do
   this even if nothing else changes.
1. Write `mem.py` + `mem` wrapper; `mem index`; run the section-6 eval against memsearch,
   rg, and `mem` on the seed set. Record the result file.
2. Point `memory-write` L1 at `mem search` (keep `memsearch search` as L1b on Mac for now);
   update `session-miner`, `closeout`, `dev-sync`, `harvest`, `backup`, `meeting-prep`,
   `ingest-book`, `library-*` SKILL.md mentions (13 skill files + 13 `~/.codex/skills` copies
   [M], 51 files total mention memsearch — grep list in Appendix B).
3. `memsearch-sync.js` worker: call `mem index` instead of `memsearch index` (seconds, no
   RAM spike, no 600 s cap needed). Same for `KeystoneOS/scripts/codex-hooks/memsearch-sync.ps1`
   and `daily-backup.ps1`'s index step.
4. Disable `\Eric\memsearch-drain-once` and `memsearch-drain-weekly` scheduled tasks.
5. Replace the `memsearch search "healthcheck"` + `docker ps` block in `stack-check.ps1`
   with `mem coverage` + a 5-question eval subset.
6. `docker compose -f ~/.memsearch/milvus/docker-compose.yml stop` (not `down`); turn off
   Docker Desktop AutoStart. Reclaims ~1.7 GB RAM and removes the "Docker must be up before
   any session ends" dependency. Leave images/volumes for 30 days.
7. After 30 clean days and one passing eval: `docker compose down -v`, `docker image prune`,
   optionally uninstall Docker Desktop (unless memsearch/Milvus is needed for something else
   — nothing else on this machine uses Docker [M: only distro is docker-desktop; Ubuntu is
   stopped]).
8. Mac: repeat 1–3 with the same script; leave `milvus.db` in place as fallback.

### 5.4 Rollback

- `config.toml` is untouched throughout. `docker compose up -d` from the same compose file
  restores the stack; re-enable AutoStart; restore the three hook lines from the `.bak`
  files the hooks already keep. The Milvus index survives in the volumes until step 7.
- If volumes were pruned: `Start-ScheduledTask -TaskPath '\Eric\' -TaskName memsearch-drain-weekly`
  rebuilds; measured 232 min for 8,764 chunks, so budget ~8 h for the full 18k [I: scaled].
- Skills keep working during rollback because `mem search` and `memsearch search` share an
  output format.

## 6. Repeatable evaluation method

Goal: a number, not a feeling, every time a model or a retrieval component changes.

### 6.1 Artifacts (all under `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/`, git-synced with the memory repo)

- `questions.jsonl` — one line per case:
  `{"id","query","keyword","expected":[basename…],"layer":"tierA|daily|transcript|vault|dev-docs","source_session","added","machine"}`.
  Seed with Appendix A (53 real queries) + the 10 pilot cases. Labelling rule: the
  expected file is the one the *session that asked* ended up reading or citing — pull it
  from the same transcript. Budget: ~30 min to label 20; grow by 5 per month from new
  sessions (the extraction script in 6.2 prints candidates).
- `recall-eval.py` — stdlib only. Backends: `memsearch`, `mem` (FTS5), `rg` (uses the
  `keyword` field), optionally `ctx` (via a tiny MCP client, or skip). Per case it records
  rank of first expected file, latency, chars returned, exit status/timeout, and
  **coverage** (does any expected file exist under the configured roots on *this* machine —
  the check that exposes path drift).
- `telemetry.py` — the 30-day transcript scan used in this audit: human vs headless
  sessions, `memsearch`/`mem`/rg/`ctx_search` call counts, hook error lines, flush
  outcomes. Cheap (streams 683 MB in ~2 min [M]).
- `results/<date>-<machine>-<model>.json` + one appended row in `ledger.md`:
  `date | machine | model | backend | n | hit@1 | hit@5 | MRR | p50 ms | p95 ms | fail% | coverage%`.

### 6.2 Metrics and decision rule

- **hit@5** (primary), hit@1, MRR; **p50/p95 latency**; **failure rate** (non-zero exit,
  timeout, backend unreachable); **coverage** (expected file reachable by the index on this
  machine); **chars returned** as the token-cost proxy.
- Retire or demote a retrieval layer when the cheaper one is within **1 hit@5 on n≥30** and
  beats it on failure rate and latency for **two consecutive runs**. Reinstate embeddings
  only if FTS5 falls >1 hit@5 behind on the same rule.
- Report per-layer, not just overall: a backend can be perfect on Tier A and useless on
  transcripts.

### 6.3 When to rerun

- Any model change in `settings.json` (`model`, `advisorModel`) or a Claude Code major.
- Any memsearch / context-mode / `mem.py` upgrade; any edit to `memory-index-paths.json`.
- Monthly via `claude-stack-doctor`'s existing `weekly-check.ps1` (run the 5-case smoke
  subset weekly, full set monthly); on both machines, so the ledger shows drift between them.

### 6.4 Where it lives

Fold into **`claude-stack-doctor`**, not the others: it already owns the memsearch smoke
test, the weekly scheduled run, the cross-machine handoff check, and the `.errors.log`
read. `doctor-plus` audits guidance-file principles, `brain-audit` scores the vault,
`improve-system` finds vault rot — none of them measure retrieval. Add two findings codes to
`stack-check.ps1`: `recall-coverage` (any configured root MISSING) and `recall-regress`
(hit@5 dropped ≥2 vs last ledger row).

| Layer | Corpus | Retrieval type | Callable from | Unique job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| memsearch + Milvus | 12 configured roots (9 reachable here), 18,360 chunks | dense (bge-m3) + keyword hybrid, chunk-level | shell → Claude Bash, Codex hooks, PowerShell scripts | Only layer with semantic matching; only one that indexes transcripts/dailies/dev-docs/codex memories together |
| context-mode (FTS5 plugin) | Whatever was captured or `ctx_index`ed: session outputs, tool results, auto-memory events (70 MB content DB) | BM25 + trigram + RRF + proximity rerank | Claude via MCP only (as tested) | Keeps large tool outputs out of context; session-timeline recall of decisions/errors. Does **not** index the memory roots unless told to |
| graphify (6 `graphify-out` dirs) | Per-repo code/docs | graph query (communities, paths, god nodes) | Claude via skill | Structure and relationships within a project; not fact recall |
| claude-memory-compiler | Writes `daily/` and `knowledge/` from transcripts; injects a pointer at start | none — it is a **writer**, not a retriever | hooks (SessionEnd/PreCompact/SessionStart) | Produces the curated daily log and 180 articles that the retrievers then search |
| Tier A memory + `MEMORY.md` index + global USER/MEMORY | ~58 notes per machine slug, 1-line index each | auto-injected (Tier 0), then Read by name | harness | Zero-cost recall for anything with a line in the index; the layer the pilot mostly exercised |
| rg / Grep over the same directories | any file on disk | exact/regex, file-level | everywhere | What the model reaches for 10× more often than memsearch [M]; no index to drift |

The overlap is between the first two and rg: three keyword-capable retrievers over
partly-overlapping corpora, plus one dense retriever whose unique contribution the pilot
could not distinguish from BM25 at n=10. graphify and the compiler do not overlap with them.

## Verdict

**1. Retire Docker/Milvus on Windows.** It exists solely because `milvus-lite` has no Windows wheel (memsearch's `store.py` says so verbatim; PyPI confirms; `import milvus_lite` fails here). The Mac runs embedded `milvus.db` with no server. Cost here: ~1.7 GB resident RAM (vmmemWSL 1.3 GB + ~0.4 GB Docker Desktop processes), 6.6–7.6 GB disk, and a daemon that must be up before any session ends. Milvus is not the latency: of memsearch's 4.4 s/query, ~0.1 s is Milvus, ~0.9 s CLI import, ~3.4 s the ONNX embedder. Swapping to sqlite-vec/LanceDB saves RAM but not time; only dropping the embedder (FTS5) does both.

**2. The single most actionable finding is coverage, not backend.** 3 of 12 configured index paths point at `~/SecondBrain/...`, which does not exist on Windows (vault is `~/Desktop/SecondBrain`). The hook filters missing paths with `existsSync` and logs nothing, so the 1,370-note vault (~1.6M tokens) has never been indexed here. Real 09-27 queries ("Zatsiorsky", "Issurin") matched 53/57 vault notes vs 8/10 indexed files; memsearch's top hit was `dev-docs/Flint/QUEUE.md`. Fix this before touching anything else.

**3. Pilot eval (10 Qs, same corpus):** memsearch 10/10 hit@5 @ 4.38 s; stdlib SQLite FTS5 9/10 @ <10 ms (17 s one-time build); rg single-keyword 8/10 @ 0.07 s. Caveat stated in the report: 9/10 questions were Tier A notes (the layer that least needs vectors). n=10 cannot rank them; it can say keyword retrieval is not obviously worse.
